The company has said it uses consumer personal information to train its ADMT — including, if applicable, an emotion-recognition, facial-recognition, or identity-verification system. The CPPA's regulations treat that training use as its own risk-assessment trigger, separate from using the ADMT to make a decision (11 CCR § 7150(b)(6)). In its Final Statement of Reasons, the CPPA explained why: training uses of personal information "pose significant risk to consumers' privacy," including the risk that the training data can later be used to re-identify the people it came from, and a general lack of transparency and control over how their information was used for training — risks the Agency said apply even where the data is not biometric. A business that trains an ADMT on real consumer data therefore has a risk-assessment obligation under Article 10 that is distinct from — and in addition to — any obligation tied to how the ADMT is later used to decide something about a consumer. This report does not itself conduct that Article 10 risk assessment; whether one has been completed is a fact about this company's own record, not something this section resolves. (California Privacy Protection Agency, Final Statement of Reasons, CCPA Updates, Cyber, Risk, ADMT, and Insurance Regulations, 11 CCR § 7150(b)(6), Appendix p. 13.)
